'''''Ipomoea indica'''''<ref>{{ITIS|id=30775|taxon=''Ipomoea indica''}}</ref> is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Convolvulaceae]], known by several common names, including '''blue morning glory''', '''oceanblue morning glory''', '''''koali awa''''', and '''blue dawn flower'''. It bears heart-shaped or three-lobed leaves and purple or blue funnel-shaped flowers {{cvt|6|-|8|cm|0}} in diameter, from [[spring (season)|spring]] to [[autumn]]. The flowers produced by the plant are [[hermaphrodite|hermaphroditic]]. This plant has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web |title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Ipomoea indica'' |url=https://rhs.org.uk/Plants/69124/Ipomoea-indica/Details |access-date=2020-09-07}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=July 2017 |title=AGM Plants - Ornamental |url=https://rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf |access-date=2018-03-12 |publisher=[[Royal Horticultural Society]] (RHS) |page=53}}</ref>

The plant is grown as an [[ornamental plant|ornamental]] for its attractive flowers, but is considered [[invasive species|invasive]] in many regions of the world, being specifically listed on New Zealand's [[Biosecurity Act 1993]].

== Etymology ==
The Latin [[Botanical name#Binary name|specific epithet]] ''indica'' means from India, or the East Indies or China.<ref name="RHSLG">{{cite book|last=Harrison|first=Lorraine|title=RHS Latin for gardeners|year=2012|publisher= [[Mitchell Beazley]] |location=United Kingdom|isbn=9781845337315|pages=224}}</ref> In this case, the name likely refers to the West Indies, as ''I. indica'' is native to the New World.

==Description==
{{refimprovesect|date=May 2024}}
[[File:Cutivated Ipomoea indica with tendrils.JPG|thumb|left|At the [[BBC Gardeners' World]] show in June 2011, with [[tendril]]s visible wrapped around the black metal support]]
[[File:Ipomoea indica (3).jpg|frameless|left|alt=Blue flowers]]
''Ipomoea indica'' is a vigorous, long-lived, [[Hardiness (plants)|tender]], [[perennial plant|perennial]] plant, a [[vine]] which is [[native plant|native]] to tropical, subtropical and warm temperate habitats throughout the world. It blooms all year long[https://books.google.com/books?id=XLFQEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22tecoma+stans%22%2B%22honey%22&pg=SA2-PA29]. They can most commonly be found in disturbed forests, forest edges, secondary woodland, suburban gullies, and along roadsides and waterways. The plant climbs well over other plants, walls and slopes as growing on the bottom. Its climbing habit allows it to compete with trees and shrubs successfully. It is a twisting, occasionally lying, [[herbaceous plant]] which is more or less densely hairy on the axial parts with backward-looking [[trichome]]s. The stems can grow {{ Convert | 3 to 6 | cm }} long and sometimes have roots at the nodes.

The leaves are petiolate with {{ Convert | 2 to 18 | cm }} long [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]]s. The leaf blade is egg-shaped or round, {{ Convert | 5 to 15 | cm }} long and {{ Convert | 3.5 to 14 | cm }} wide. The underside is densely hairy with short, soft trichomes, the top is more or less sparsely hairy. The base is heart-shaped, the leaf margin is entire or three-lobed, the tip is pointed or sharply pointed.

The [[crown (botany)|crown]] is funnel-shaped, {{ Convert | 5 to 8 | cm }} long, [[Glabrousness (botany)|glabrous]], bright blue or bluish purple, with age they become reddish purple or red. The centre of the crown is a little paler.

''I. indica'' is a long-lived plant that can live up to 25 years.<ref name=":0" />

===Inflorescence and fruit===
The [[inflorescence]]s are dense, umbelliform [[Cyme (botany)|cyme]]s from a few flowers. The inflorescence stems are {{ Convert | 4 to 20 | cm }} long. The [[bract]]s are linear or sometimes lanceolate. The flower stems are {{ Convert | 2 to 5 | mm }} (rarely up to {{ Convert | 8 | mm }}) long. The [[sepal]]s are almost uniform, 1.4 to 2.2 cm long and slowly sharpened linearly. They are hairless to close-fitting, the outer three sepals are lanceolate to broadly lanceolate, and the inner two are narrowly lanceolate. The [[stamen]]s and the stamp do not protrude beyond the crown. The [[Ovary (botany)|ovary]] is hairless. The scar is three-lobed. The flowers [[Floral color change|change colour]], where they start out as bright blue early in the morning, shifting to a darker shade of blue in midday, then to a [[periwinkle (color)|lavender blue]] and finally to a deep pink at the end of the day.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Malloy|first=Mike|date=2016-04-15|title=Morning glory's beauty part of glorious morning, colorful day|publisher=[[Naples Daily News]]}}</ref>

The fruits are more or less spherical capsules with a diameter of {{ Convert | 1 to 1.3 | cm }}. The seeds are about {{ Convert | 5 | mm }} in size and are dispersed via rain, wind, [[Hemerochory|human activity]], gravity, and waterways.

Flowering and fruiting are dependent on location. Some countries, such as [[Costa Rica]] and [[Nicaragua]], observe year round flowering and fruiting while other countries like [[South Africa]] observe fruiting and flowering that is constrained to specific months.<ref name=":0" /> Generally however, they bloom throughout the year,<ref>[https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/weeds/data/media/Html/ipomoea_indica.htm ''Ipomoea indica'' (Burm.) Merr.] Lucid Central, Weeds of Australia.</ref> but much more profusely so from late spring to fall.<ref>[https://www.gardenia.net/plant/ipomoea-indica-blue-morning-glory ''Ipomoea indica'' (Blue Morning Glory)] Gardenia.net</ref>

==Taxonomy and phylogenetics==
[[Image:Bons-dias (Ipomoea indica) em terreno baldio em Bagé - 54958650515.jpg|thumb|Single flower in Brazil]]
''[[Ipomoea]]'' is a large and diverse genus containing between 600–1,000 species, with 820 being recognized by the [[Catalogue of Life]].{{r|col_ipomoea}} Although the genus as a whole is not [[monophyletic]], ''I. indica'' belongs to a well-supported clade of the ''Pharbitis'' section in the ''Quamoclit'' subgenus. A 2014 phylogenetic study on 36 members of the ''Quamoclit'' subgenus (30% of the species). The results suggest ''I. indica's ''closest living relatives to be the [[Ipomoea hederacea|ivy-leaved]] and [[Ipomoea nil|picotee]] morning glories.{{r|miller2004ajb}}

== Distribution ==
[[File:0753_-_Taormina_-_Convolvolo_-_Foto_di_Giovanni_DallOrto_-_30-Sept-2006.jpg|frameless|right|alt=Growing down a wall]]
[[File:Ipomoea indica.jpg|thumb|[[Uruguay]]|alt=Purple flowers in [[Uruguay]]]]
Its exact native distribution is unclear due to it being widely cultivated throughout the tropics of Eurasia, Africa and America, but it is currently thought by most authorities to be native to the [[Neotropical realm|Neotropics]], from [[Florida]]<ref>{{Cite web|title= ''Ipomoea indica'' - Species Details|url=http://florida.plantatlas.usf.edu/plant.aspx?id=3387|access-date=2020-12-12|website= [[Atlas of Florida Plants]] }}</ref> in the [[United States]] south to [[Mexico]], [[Central America]], and the [[Caribbean]] and south to [[South America]]. It is also considered native to several [[List of islands in the Pacific Ocean|Pacific islands]], including [[Palau]], the [[Hawaiian Islands|Hawaiian Archipelago]] (where its [[Hawaiian language|native Hawaiian]] name is ''Koali ‘awa''),<ref>{{Cite web|date=2018-05-22|title=Koali 'awa (''Ipomoea indica'')|url=http://kureatollconservancy.org/koali-awa/|access-date=2020-12-12|website=Kure Atoll Conservancy|language=en-US|archive-date=2021-01-16|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210116085630/http://kureatollconservancy.org/koali-awa/|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Native Plants Hawaii - Viewing Plant : ''Ipomoea indica''|url=http://www.nativeplants.hawaii.edu/plant/view/Ipomoea_indica|access-date=2020-12-12|website=www.nativeplants.hawaii.edu|archive-date=2020-02-25|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200225025900/http://www.nativeplants.hawaii.edu/plant/view/Ipomoea_indica|url-status=dead}}</ref> [[French Polynesia]], and [[Micronesia]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title= ''Ipomoea indica'' (ocean blue morning-glory)|url=https://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/107833|access-date=2020-12-12|website= [[Centre for Agriculture and Bioscience International|CABI]] (Centre for Agriculture and Bioscience International) |language=en}}</ref>

However, other authorities consider it to be an introduced and/or invasive species in the United States, Mexico, and parts of its Caribbean and Pacific range.<ref name=":0" />

== Invasive species ==
''Ipomoea indica'' has become a noxious weed and [[invasive species|invasive plant species]] in [[Australia]], [[California]], [[China]], [[Ethiopia]], [[France]], [[Greece]], [[Italy]], [[Kenya]],  [[Mexico]], [[Montenegro]],<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Bubanja|first=Nada|title=Five new alien species in the flora of Montenegro: ''Coreopsis tinctoria'' Nutt., ''Ipomoea indica'' (Burm.) Merr., ''Lupinus'' × ''regalis'' Bergmans, ''Physalis angulata'' L., and ''Solidago canadensis'' L. and new possible threats to the biodiversity|journal= [[Acta Botanica Croatica]] |volume=76|pages=98–102}}</ref> [[New Caledonia]],<ref>{{Cite book|last=Hequet|first=Vanessa|url=http://horizon.documentation.ird.fr/exl-doc/pleins_textes/divers12-08/010052239.pdf|title=Les espèces exotiques envahissantes de Nouvelle-Calédonie|year=2009|pages=17|language=fr}}</ref> [[New Zealand]], [[Portugal]],<ref>Plantas invasoras em Portugal (2013). ''Ipomoea indica''. Available in http://invasoras.uc.pt/gallery/ipomoea-indica/. Accessed on 28 July 2013.</ref> [[South Africa]], [[Tanzania]], and [[Uganda]]. In New Zealand, it is classed as an unwanted organism under the [[Biosecurity Act 1993]] and it is therefore illegal to sell, propagate and distribute the plant.<ref>{{cite web|date=20 March 2009|title=Blue morning glory|url=http://www.biosecurity.govt.nz/pests/blue-morning-glory|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100527011620/http://www.biosecurity.govt.nz/pests/blue-morning-glory|archive-date=27 May 2010|access-date=31 July 2010|publisher=Biosecurity New Zealand}}</ref> It is listed on the [[National Pest Plant Accord]] for New Zealand.

When growing in optimal conditions, the plant is able to spread via seeds, [[stolon]]s, and stem fragments. ''I. indica'' is capable of producing a very large amounts of seeds for dispersal. These seeds are easily germinated, giving the plant the ability to rapidly invade and colonize new land. It can grow over pre-existing trees, shrubs, and other plant species. ''I. indica'' successfully outcompetes many native plants for substrates, nutrients, sunlight and water. The stolons of blue morning glory create a thick mat over ground plants, reducing the light available for those plants. The stolons of blue morning glory are also capable of growing at a rapid pace, adding to the plant's [[Ecological succession|succession]].<ref name=":0" /> Each part can grow as a separate plant if snapped during the process of attempted removal.

The only natural enemy of ''I. indica'' is the oomycete plant pathogen ''[[Albugo ipomoeae-panduratae]],'' which have shown instances of infecting the plant. Its lack of natural enemies is another reason ''I. indica'' is very successful and adds to its invasive abilities.<ref name=":0" />

==Cultivation==
Blue morning glory is a popular species widely cultivated as an ornamental plant for its colourful flowers. It has spread throughout the tropics and subtropics of the [[Old World]] although those regions are not part of its native range. As it does not tolerate temperatures below {{convert|7|C|F|abbr=on}}, in [[temperateness|temperate]] regions it is grown under glass.<ref name=RHSAZ>{{cite book|title=RHS A-Z encyclopedia of garden plants|year=2008|publisher=Dorling Kindersley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=978-1405332965|pages=1136}}</ref> It likes very light and nutrient-rich soil, which should be kept evenly moist.{{original research inline|date=May 2024}}
===Uses===
''Ipomoea indica'' is an ideal plant for honey production because it blooms all year long<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=XLFQEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22tecoma+stans%22%2B%22honey%22&pg=SA2-PA29 Honey: A Miraculous Product of Nature.]</ref>
